summary: The Internet Printing Protocol is an application-level protocol for distributed printing. This document, an internet standard, describes a simplified model of abstract objects, attributes and operations, independent of encoding and transport, such as printers and jobs.

eli5.summary: This part of the printing standard explains the main ideas: printers, print jobs, and what you can ask them to do, without worrying about how messages travel.

questions: what is the internet printing protocol
what are the ipp job states
subtitle: The abstract printing model behind IPP: Printers, Jobs, the operations on them and the attributes that describe them.

tldr.problem: Printing over a network involves drivers, spoolers, servers and many kinds of output devices, so clients need one simple, device-independent way to find a printer, submit work and watch it.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Printing Protocol models printing as two main objects, a Printer and a Job, and defines synchronous request/response operations and typed attributes on them, independent of encoding and transport.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8011 is the IPP/1.1 Model and Semantics specification. It obsoletes RFC 2911, RFC 3381 and RFC 3382, and is paired with RFC 8010 for encoding and transport.

today: RFC 8011 is an Internet Standard published in January 2017 and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 2911, RFC 3381 and RFC 3382, and is meant to be read with RFC 8010, which covers encoding and transport.

sections.title: Introduction and the Simplified Model
sections.content:
The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application-level protocol for distributed printing using Internet tools and technologies. IPP/1.1 focuses primarily on End User functionality, with a few administrative operations. IPP versions 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2 add many new operations and are defined separately. This document is one of a suite, and the message encoding and transport are in RFC 8010.

Real print systems have many parts, so IPP is based on a simplified printing model that exposes only the key objects and interfaces. The model has four object types: Printer, Job, Document and Subscription. A Printer folds together what a physical output device does with the spooling, scheduling and multiple-device management often found in a print server. A Client sends IPP requests to it on behalf of an End User.

Every IPP operation is synchronous: each has a request and a response. Users can poll with Get-Printer-Attributes, Get-Jobs and Get-Job-Attributes, or use the separate notification service defined in RFC 3995 to receive events asynchronously.
sections.eli5: Printing at an office has lots of moving parts. IPP pretends there are only two main things, the printer and your print job, so asking a printer for anything works the same way every time.

sections.title: Printer and Job Objects
sections.content:
A Printer object implements the server side of IPP/1.1. It can be embedded in an output device, hosted on a server in front of one output device, or fan out to several. Because it is an abstraction, it can represent any real or virtual device with matching semantics, such as a fax device, an imager or even a CD writer. A Printer contains zero or more Jobs.

A Job object models one print job. It holds zero or more Documents, where a Document is either a stream of document data in a format the Printer supports (typically a page description language) or a reference to such a stream. An implementation MUST support at least one Document per Job and MAY support several. A Job is contained by exactly one Printer.

Each object type is defined as a set of possible attributes. Every attribute is labeled REQUIRED (each object MUST support it), RECOMMENDED (SHOULD) or OPTIONAL (MAY). Printer attributes fall into job-template and printer-description groups; Job attributes into job-template and job-description groups. All the processing instructions for a Job are modeled as Job Template attributes, and they apply equally to every Document in the Job.
sections.eli5: A printer is like a bakery counter, and each order you place there is a job. An order can hold one item or several, and your instructions, like how many copies, apply to the whole order.

sections.title: Identifying Printers and Jobs
sections.content:
Every IPP object is identified by a URI. A Printer lists its URIs in the multi-valued printer-uri-supported attribute, which MUST contain at least one value. Two companion attributes, uri-security-supported and uri-authentication-supported, have the same number of values and say which security and authentication mechanism goes with each URI. A Client names exactly one Printer URI in a request, and it MUST be one of the listed values. IPP/1.1 does not say how a Client finds the URI, though it RECOMMENDS registering Printers in a directory service.

When the Printer creates a Job it assigns a numeric job-id, a 32-bit positive integer that is unique only within that Printer, and a job-uri. The numeric identifier is preferred, and use of job-uri by Clients is DEPRECATED. Clients SHOULD target a Job with the printer-uri and job-id attributes, which avoids any doubt about the security of the channel. The Job also carries job-printer-uri, a link back to the Printer that created it.

Names are separate from identity. printer-name and job-name are not guaranteed to be unique and have only local meaning. If the Client gives no Job name, the Printer generates one.
sections.eli5: A printer has an address, like a street address, and each job gets a ticket number from that printer. The number only means something at that printer, just like a bakery ticket number.

sections.title: Operations and Common Semantics
sections.content:
An operation is a request plus a response. Every request carries a version-number, an operation-id and a request-id. The Client picks the request-id as an integer from 1 to 2**31 - 1 so it can match responses to outstanding requests. Every response carries a version-number, a status-code and the request-id from the request.

The first two operation attributes in every request and response MUST be attributes-charset and attributes-natural-language, in that order. They say how text and name values are encoded and which language they use. All Clients and IPP objects MUST support the utf-8 charset, so Clients are advised to send it. Individual values in another language use the Natural Language Override mechanism, which every object and Client MUST support. After these come the target attributes: printer-uri, plus job-id for most Job operations.

Versions are written X.Y. There is no version negotiation per se. An object that does not support the major version replies with server-error-version-not-supported and the closest version it does support, and an IPP/1.1 object MUST support version 1.1. Responses also carry a status-message (up to 255 octets, aimed at people) and may carry a detailed-status-message, which Clients MUST NOT parse.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with the same few lines, like a letter that always begins with who it is from and what language it is written in. Because the opening is always the same, both sides can read the rest.

sections.title: Submitting and Managing Jobs
sections.content:
A Client creates a Job with one of three Job Creation operations. Print-Job (REQUIRED) pushes a single Document in the request. Print-URI (OPTIONAL) sends only a URI that the Printer pulls the data from. Create-Job (RECOMMENDED) makes a Job with no data, and is followed by any number of Send-Document or Send-URI operations. The last one carries last-document set to true. Clients SHOULD prefer Create-Job and Send-Document when supported, because they allow monitoring and control while the data is being sent. Validate-Job (REQUIRED) runs the same checks as Print-Job but creates no Job.

At submission time the Printer MUST validate the supplied attributes against its xxx-supported attributes and check the syntax and scheme of any URI. Problems found later, while processing, cannot be returned as an operation status, so the Printer records them in job-state, job-state-reasons or job-state-message. A Printer short on space can answer server-error-busy and should show the spool-space-full reason.

To follow up, Get-Printer-Attributes, Get-Jobs and Get-Job-Attributes are REQUIRED queries. In Get-Jobs, which-jobs defaults to not-completed and my-jobs defaults to false. Cancel-Job is REQUIRED. Hold-Job, Release-Job, Pause-Printer and Resume-Printer are OPTIONAL, and Pause-Printer and Resume-Printer must be supported together.
sections.eli5: You can hand the printer your whole document at once, give it a web address to fetch, or open an order first and add pages one by one. After that you can ask how your order is doing or cancel it.

sections.title: The Job Life Cycle
sections.content:
The REQUIRED job-state attribute has seven values. A Job starts as pending, pending-held or processing. It normally moves from left to right through processing to one of three terminal states: completed, canceled or aborted. processing-stopped is a pause that returns to processing when the cause clears. Implementations only need to support the states that suit their output device. The job-state-reasons attribute adds detail, for example job-printing, processing-to-stop-point or completed-successfully.

After a Job reaches a terminal state, it passes through phases. In Job Retention the Printer MAY keep the document data restartable for an implementation-defined time, which may be zero. In Job History the data is deleted but the Job stays visible, and Printers SHOULD keep it there for at least 60 seconds. After Job Removal, no operation can return anything about it.

The Printer has its own printer-state: idle (3), processing (4) or stopped (5), refined by printer-state-reasons.
sections.eli5: A print job is like a parcel on a trip. It waits, gets worked on, and ends up delivered, cancelled or lost. Sometimes it is put on hold or stopped for a while on the way.

sections.title: Job Template Attributes
sections.content:
Job Template attributes are the knobs a Client can set on a Job: job-priority, job-hold-until, job-sheets, multiple-document-handling, copies, finishings, page-ranges, sides, number-up, orientation-requested, media, printer-resolution and print-quality. Most have a matching xxx-default and xxx-supported attribute on the Printer, so a Client can ask what is available before submitting.

A Printer supports an attribute only if it accepts it in a request or returns it populated in a query. If a Printer can staple but does not list staple in finishings-supported, then as far as IPP is concerned it does not support stapling. An Administrator can also hide features by listing only some values. Support for Job Template attributes is OPTIONAL, but a Printer whose device can do something SHOULD support the matching attribute and value.

For example, job-priority runs from 1 (lowest) to 100 (highest), and a Printer that supports it MUST support the full range. If it offers only n priority levels, it maps the Client value onto n evenly spread values; for n = 3 these are 17, 50 and 83. Appendix C also sketches the order in which attributes shape document processing: page selection, number-up, sides, copies, then finishings.

Attribute values use defined syntaxes such as text (at most 1023 octets), keyword, enum, uri and boolean. Three out-of-band values can replace a value: unknown, unsupported and no-value.
sections.eli5: Job settings are like the choices on an order form: how many copies, one side or two sides, which paper. The printer also publishes a menu of what it can really do.

sections.title: Unsupported Attributes and Fidelity
sections.content:
A Client may ask for something the Printer cannot do. Unsupported attributes fall into three kinds: the Printer does not support the attribute at all, it supports the attribute but not the particular value, or the values are supported separately but conflict, such as stapling transparencies. The Printer reports them in an Unsupported Attributes group. For an unknown attribute name, it echoes the attribute with the out-of-band value unsupported. For a bad value, it echoes the value as supplied.

Whether the Job is still accepted depends on the ipp-attribute-fidelity boolean. With true, the Client wants total fidelity and the Printer MUST reject the request if it cannot print exactly as specified. With false, or when omitted, the Printer MUST accept the request, ignoring unsupported attributes and substituting supported values. In the RFC's example, a request for na_letter_8.5x11in media may be answered with iso_a4_210x297mm. Every Printer MUST support both modes.

Instructions may also be embedded in the document data. IPP attribute values SHOULD take precedence, but whether a Printer can manage that is advertised in the REQUIRED pdl-override-supported attribute, with the values attempted and not-attempted. Not every unsupported value is a clean status code; for requests that name an unsupported version, charset, compression or document format, Table 1 maps each to its own error status code.
sections.eli5: Imagine ordering a pizza with a topping the shop does not have. You can say, only make it exactly this way or not at all, or you can say, just make me something nice. The printer follows whichever you pick.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it is hard to anticipate the risks in any given IPP environment. On a private office network the risk of exposing document data may be low enough to skip encryption, while a connection over a public network can protect content with encryption. Denial-of-service attacks against printing resources are described as not well understood, with no published precedents.

IPP objects authenticate the requester, record that user as the job-originating-user-name (the Job owner) and then enforce whatever authorization policy the site has. Each Printer URI has its own authentication mechanism in uri-authentication-supported; with mechanism none, all users are anonymous. Cancel-Job and the other Job operations are intended for the Job owner or an Operator or Administrator. Pause-Printer, Resume-Printer and Purge-Jobs are intended for Operators and Administrators, and others MUST be rejected with client-error-forbidden, client-error-not-authenticated or client-error-not-authorized.

An object can be configured to return fewer attributes than a Client asks for, for example hiding another user's Job details, and the status returned is the same as if everything had been returned. For print by reference, standard methods for passing a Client's credentials to a third party do not exist, so it is expected to be used for public documents. Clients MUST support Client Authentication as defined in RFC 8010 and SHOULD support Operation Privacy and Server Authentication.
sections.eli5: A printer should know who is asking before it lets someone cancel a job or pause the whole machine. Normally only the person who sent a job, or the office helper in charge, can change it.

sections.title: Conformance, Extensions and Changes
sections.content:
A conforming IPP object MUST implement every REQUIRED operation and attribute, and may support any non-empty subset of the values an attribute allows. It MUST ignore unknown operation attributes but reject a supported attribute that carries an unsupported value. Clients, in turn, MUST gracefully handle extra groups, attributes and values in responses rather than refuse to interoperate with a conforming Printer.

The IPP registries kept by IANA cover objects, attributes, keyword and enum values, attribute group tags, out-of-band tags, attribute syntaxes, operations and status codes. Vendors are told to prefix their own attribute keywords with smiNNN-, where NNN is an SMI Private Enterprise Number.

Compared with RFC 2911, this document fixes several errata, makes Create-Job, Send-Document and Send-URI RECOMMENDED, and folds in the collection syntax from RFC 3382. It obsoletes all attributes and values from RFC 3381, which interact badly with finishings and were never widely implemented. It deprecates Purge-Jobs and Restart-Job because they destroy accounting information, so both are now SHOULD NOT.
sections.eli5: There is a checklist of what every printer must be able to do and what is optional. Makers can add their own special features, as long as they label them so nothing gets mixed up.

items.label: pending
items.desc: A candidate to start processing, but not yet processing.

items.label: pending-held
items.desc: Not a candidate for processing; returns to pending when the reasons clear.

items.label: processing
items.desc: Being worked on or queued at the output device.

items.label: processing-stopped
items.desc: Stopped while processing; returns to processing when the reasons clear.

items.label: canceled
items.desc: Canceled by Cancel-Job and the Printer has finished canceling.

items.label: completed
items.desc: Finished, with success, warnings or errors.

viz.caption: MULTI-STEP JOB CREATION (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC)

messages.label: Create-Job
messages.note: No document data; the Printer creates an empty Job.

messages.label: Response
messages.note: Includes a job-id, as with Print-Job.

messages.label: Send-Document
messages.note: Carries document data for the Job.

messages.label: Send-Document, last-document true
messages.note: The final request marks the end of the Job's documents.

left.title: fidelity = true
left.desc: Print exactly as specified. If the Printer cannot, it MUST reject the request.

right.title: fidelity = false (default)
right.desc: Make a reasonable attempt. The Printer MUST accept, ignoring or substituting what it does not support.
